561.title: Chosen, not born
561.hook: the people choose one to govern them: a gentle satire of caste origins
561.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Agganna Sutta when they teach that a person's worth comes from conduct, not birth, and the sutta itself says someone from any of the four classes can go forth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shining beings and a sweet crust, and your line, they tasted the earth. Did you catch the moment wanting turned into more? Today the same story arrives at its first ruler. Day five hundred sixty-one.

The story in the Agganna Sutta moves on. After the savory earth comes a kind of fungus, then a creeper, and then rice that grows wild and ripens again overnight. Then someone gets lazy: why go out twice a day? I'll bring in enough for two meals. Others copy him, gathering for two days, then four, then eight. Soon the rice stops regrowing. So they divide the land into fields, with boundaries. And then one being, greedy again, guards his own plot and takes from someone else's. He's caught. He promises not to do it again. He does it again. Today: chosen.
screen: `RICE THAT RIPENS OVERNIGHT.` → `ENOUGH FOR EIGHT DAYS.` → `FIELDS, BOUNDARIES, THEFT.`

segments.voice: Theft appears, then blame, then lying, then punishment with sticks. So the beings gather and talk it over. What if we picked one of us, someone who'd be angry when anger is right, blame what deserves blame, and banish who deserves banishing? And we'd each give that person a share of rice. They choose the best-looking, most pleasant, most capable among them. Notice: chosen, by agreement. Not born to it, not sent down from heaven. The sutta then gives each title a punning origin. He's called Mahasammata, the great elect, because the people chose him. He's called khattiya, a noble, because he's lord of the fields. He's called raja, a king, because he delights people by doing what's right. Then the brahmins: those who put away bad things, says the text. Some went to the forest to meditate. Others couldn't manage meditation and settled near villages compiling books, and were called non-meditators. The wordplay is gentle, and it's aimed at a claim about birth, not at anyone's faith. These derivations are wordplay, not dictionary etymology, and some scholars read them as deliberate satire. The point lands at the end. People from any of the four classes can act badly, and people from any class can act well and be freed. And the Buddha closes by quoting a verse he agrees with: the noble is best among those who care about clan, but one with knowledge and good conduct is best among gods and humans.
screen: `THEY GATHER AND TALK IT OVER.` · `MAHASAMMATA: THE GREAT ELECT.` · `TITLES AS WORDPLAY.` · `ANY CLASS, GOOD OR BAD.` · then, large: `CHOSEN, NOT BORN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who leads fairly: a manager, a coach, a teacher, an elected official you respect, the person who keeps your family or your team together. Picture them doing the ordinary job well, settling a quarrel, sharing out the work. Let some gratitude come up for them. Then notice: they weren't born to that. Someone trusted them with it. The bell holds the time.
Chosen. In DN 27 the first ruler is chosen by the people, the great elect, and the old class titles are told with a wink. Today's word.
Your line: chosen, not born. Today, thank or honor one person who leads fairly, and notice what they do, not where they come from. Day five hundred sixty-one.

fork.setup: theft and fighting have started among the first people. what do they do in the story?
options: each family arms itself.
they gather and choose one capable person to govern, paid in rice.
they wait for a god to send a king.
fork.reveal: they choose the most capable among them, the great elect, and each give him a share of rice.

original.note: Pali Mahasammata: the great elect, the first ruler chosen by the people in DN 27.

trapdoor: what you thought: ancient kings always claimed a right by birth or by heaven.
what it means: in DN 27 the first ruler is chosen by the people and paid for the job.

what a scholar hears: the Agganna's punning etymologies (khattiya from khetta, raja from ranjeti) are often read as satire of brahmanical origin claims, and Mahasammata later became a royal ancestor in Buddhist chronicles.

562.title: What I trust
562.hook: Sariputta's lion's roar of confidence in the Buddha
562.howItsDone: Buddhists describe saddha, faith or confidence, as one of the five spiritual faculties, and many teachers explain it as trust that grows through testing the teaching in one's own practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first ruler, chosen by the people, and your line, chosen, not born. Who did you honor for leading fairly? Today a great disciple makes a bold claim, and gets questioned for it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

People say things like it. She's the best doctor in the world. This is the greatest band that ever lived. It comes out of love, and it's usually more than we could prove. Sariputta, the disciple known for wisdom, comes to the Buddha at Nalanda and says something like that. Sir, I'm so confident in you that I believe there has never been, will never be, and is not now anyone who surpasses you in awakening. It's called a lion's roar. And the Buddha doesn't just smile and accept the compliment. Today: what I trust.
screen: `THE BEST IN THE WORLD.` → `SARIPUTTA'S LION'S ROAR.` → `THE BUDDHA DOESN'T JUST ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Sampasadaniya, the one that inspires confidence, the twenty-eighth. The Buddha answers with questions. Lofty words, Sariputta. Have you known the minds of all the Buddhas of the past? No, sir. Of all the Buddhas to come? No, sir. Of me, right now, so that you could say exactly what my virtue and wisdom are? No, sir. Then why such a bold roar? It's a fair challenge, and Sariputta takes it honestly. He doesn't claim to know what he doesn't. Instead he says: I know it by the way the teaching goes. The Blessed One taught me step by step, each stage finer than the last, and as I understood it, my confidence in the teacher grew. When the same conversation is told in the account of the last journey, Sariputta adds a picture. A king's frontier town has strong walls and only one gate, and a wise gatekeeper walks all the way around and finds no gap, not even one big enough for a cat to slip through. He doesn't need to count every creature that comes in. Anything large enough to matter comes through the one gate. So too, Sariputta says, every awakened one, past, future and present, passes through the same gate: letting go of the hindrances, establishing mindfulness, developing the factors of awakening. Back in the Sampasadaniya, he goes on to list, one by one, what he has found well taught. Look at what happens to his confidence. It doesn't shrink. It changes shape. From I know everything to here is what I've checked, and here is why I trust it. In Pali the word is pasada: a clear, settled confidence, like water after the mud has sunk.
screen: `HAVE YOU KNOWN ALL THEIR MINDS?` · `NO, SIR. BUT I KNOW THE WAY.` · `ONE GATE, NO GAP FOR A CAT.` · `PASADA: CLEAR, SETTLED CONFIDENCE.` · then, large: `WHAT I TRUST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and name to yourself one thing you trust. A person, a practice, a teaching, a friendship. Then ask the Buddha's question: what do I actually know about it? And Sariputta's answer: what have I checked for myself? Let the confidence settle, like muddy water going clear. If it's still there when the water is clear, say quietly what you trust and why. The bell holds the time.
What I trust. In DN 28 Sariputta's confidence is questioned, and he grounds it in what he has understood of the teaching, like a gatekeeper who knows his walls. Today's word.
Your line: what I trust. Today, tell one person something you trust, and the plain reason you trust it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

what it means: in DN 28 confidence is questioned, and rests on what has been checked.

what a scholar hears: in DN 28 Sariputta grounds his roar in the way the Dhamma goes (dhammanvaya); DN 16 and SN 47.12 tell the same exchange with the frontier-town simile, where the 'gate' is the abandoning of the hindrances, satipatthana and the bojjhangas.

563.title: Well proclaimed
563.hook: a teaching well proclaimed survives its teacher's death
563.tomorrow: The marks of a great man
563.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics in many traditions still memorize and chant the discourses together, and the great councils of the tradition, from the first after the Buddha's death to modern ones, were recitations checked in common.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta's confidence, and your line, what I trust. Did you say what you trust, and why? Today, news arrives of a teacher's death, and a worry about what happens next. Day five hundred sixty-three.

A young novice named Cunda has spent the rainy season near the town of Pava, and he has watched something unravel there. A well-known teacher of the time, Nigantha Nataputta, has died, and his followers have split into camps, each telling the other it has the teaching wrong. When the rains end, Cunda walks to Samagama, where Ananda is staying, and tells him everything. Ananda listens. He doesn't pass the story along. He thinks of his own community, and says: friend Cunda, this is worth bringing to the Blessed One. Let's go and tell him. Today: well proclaimed.
screen: `A NOVICE AT PAVA.` → `A COMMUNITY SPLITS.` → `ANANDA: TAKE THIS TO THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Nigantha Nataputta is the teacher the Jain tradition honors as Mahavira, and Jains tell the story of his passing in their own texts and their own way. The Pasadika Sutta, the pleasing discourse, uses the news only as a starting point and turns to the Buddha's own followers. What keeps a teaching alive after its teacher dies? The Buddha's answer has two parts. First, it has to be well proclaimed: clearly taught, complete, its meaning made plain, so that students aren't left guessing. Second, the students have to keep it that way. And then he gives them a job. Come together, all of you, and recite what I have taught, comparing meaning with meaning and wording with wording, so that this holy life may last long, for the welfare of many. He even explains what to do when someone gets it wrong. If a fellow student recites a teaching and the wording seems off, or the meaning, don't applaud and don't scorn. Ask, gently: friend, which fits better, this wording or that one? This meaning or that one? Keep asking until it's clear. It's the habit of the four great references from a couple of weeks ago, now practiced together, out loud, kindly. And it's why the discourses still exist. For centuries they were not written down at all. They were carried by people sitting together, reciting, checking each other, and keeping the words clear. A teaching well proclaimed, held by students who keep proclaiming it well.
screen: `NEWS OF A TEACHER'S PASSING.` · `TAUGHT CLEARLY, AND COMPLETE.` · `RECITE IT TOGETHER.` · `FRIEND, WHICH FITS BETTER?` · then, large: `WELL PROCLAIMED.`

segments.voice: Choose one teaching you care about, from this path or anywhere, and say it to yourself as clearly as you can, in one sentence. Then ask the sutta's gentle question: is this the right wording? Is this the right meaning? Adjust it. Say it again. Then let it go and sit with the breath, the teaching resting clear in the background. The bell holds the time.
Well proclaimed. In DN 29 the Buddha says a clearly taught teaching, kept clear by students reciting together, survives its teacher. Today's word.
Your line: well proclaimed. Today, if you pass on something you've learned, say it clearly, and if someone gets it slightly wrong, ask gently which fits better. Day five hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 563 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MARKS OF A GREAT MAN.`

options: spread the news around the monastery.
take it to the Buddha, thinking of your own community's future.

fork.reveal: Ananda says it's worth bringing to the Blessed One, and the Buddha teaches how a teaching stays whole: recite it together.

original.note: Pali svakkhata: well proclaimed. the first word of the classic praise of the Dhamma.

trapdoor: what you thought: teachings survive because they're written down.
what it means: in DN 29 they survive by being taught clearly and recited together, checked kindly.
what a scholar hears: DN 29 and DN 33 both open with the Nigantha schism at Pava and urge communal recitation (sangayana), the same word later used for the Buddhist councils.

564.title: The marks of a great man
564.word: The marks of a great man
564.hook: the thirty-two marks and the good deeds said to cause them, read as poetry
564.howItsDone: Buddhist images across Asia show some of the thirty-two marks, most visibly the urna between the brows and the ushnisha on the crown, and teachers often explain each mark through the deed the Lakkhana Sutta links to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a teaching that outlives its teacher, and your line, well proclaimed. Did you pass something on clearly? Today, an old list that's easy to misread, about a body. Day five hundred sixty-four.

Look closely at an old statue of the Buddha. There's a small round mark between the eyebrows. A rounded swelling on the crown of the head. Sometimes a wheel carved on the sole of each foot. These aren't decorations a sculptor made up. They come from a list of thirty-two marks of a great man, signs that a person will become either a world ruler or a Buddha. The thirtieth Long Discourse, the Lakkhana Sutta, takes that list and asks a different question. Not what the marks are. Where they come from. Today: the marks of a great man.
screen: `A MARK BETWEEN THE EYEBROWS.` → `THIRTY-TWO MARKS.` → `WHERE DO THEY COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The Lakkhana Sutta goes through the marks in groups, and for each it tells what the Buddha did in earlier lives to earn it. Then it repeats the whole thing in verse. Here are a few. The wheels on the soles of his feet: because in past lives he brought happiness to many, took away fear and danger, and gave protection. Soft, tender hands, and fingers said to be webbed or net-like: because he drew people together in four ways, by giving, by kind words, by helpful action, and by treating people as equals. Deep blue eyes and lashes like a cow's: because he looked at people kindly, straight and openly, not sideways, not with suspicion. And the soft white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the mark you see on statues: because he refused to lie. Read it that way and the list stops being strange. It becomes a portrait. A body shaped, over many lives, by what it did. Feet that carried people out of danger. Hands that gave and gathered. Eyes that looked kindly. A face that told the truth. Readers have taken the marks in different ways, as physical signs, as symbols, or as both. The sutta's point holds either way: deeds leave marks. And there's a kind of marking anyone can see in an ordinary face. The lines of someone who has smiled a lot. The steady eyes of someone who doesn't lie to you.
screen: `WHEELS: BRINGING PEOPLE HAPPINESS.` · `SOFT HANDS: GIVING AND GATHERING.` · `KIND EYES: LOOKING STRAIGHT.` · `THE TUFT: TELLING THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE MARKS OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind a kind face you know. Someone whose kindness shows. Look at it in your mind's eye. Where does the kindness live? In the eyes, the mouth, the way they tilt their head? Stay with that face for a while. Then, gently, feel your own face. Soften the eyes. Let the jaw loosen. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
The marks of a great man. In DN 30 each of the thirty-two marks is traced to a good deed: kind eyes from looking kindly, the tuft from telling the truth. Today's word.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A GREAT MAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the marks of kindness. Today, notice one kind face, and let yours look at people the way the sutta says: straight, open and kind. Day five hundred sixty-four.

and taking away fear and giving protection.

fork.reveal: the tuft, the urna, is linked to truthful speech in past lives.

original.note: Pali lakkhana: mark, sign, characteristic. the thirty-two mahapurisa-lakkhana, marks of a great man.

trapdoor: what you thought: the marks on Buddha statues are just artistic style.
what it means: they come from a list of thirty-two marks, and DN 30 ties each to a deed of kindness.

what a scholar hears: DN 30 says seers outside the order knew the marks but not their causes; it pairs each mark with past-life conduct in prose and then verse, and the four sangaha-vatthu appear as the cause of the hand marks.

565.title: A protective chant
565.hook: a verse of protection given by the spirit kings
565.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks chant paritta verses at blessings, illnesses and new beginnings, often holding a white cord that links everyone present, and the Atanatiya verses are part of the larger paritta collection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thirty-two marks traced to good deeds, and your line, the marks of kindness. Whose kind face did you notice? Today, four kings arrive at night with a gift for monks alone in the forest. Day five hundred sixty-five.

It's late at night on Vulture's Peak, above Rajagaha. The hill lights up. The Four Great Kings have come, the guardians of the four directions in Buddhist cosmology, each with a vast retinue of spirits. Vessavana, guardian of the north, speaks for them. Some spirits trust the Buddha's teaching, he says, and some don't. And your monks and nuns live alone, in forests and empty places, where those spirits roam. So we've brought something. A verse they can say, to stay safe and at ease. Today: a protective chant.
screen: `NIGHT ON VULTURE'S PEAK.` → `THE FOUR GREAT KINGS ARRIVE.` → `A GIFT FOR THOSE ALONE.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Atanatiya Sutta, the thirty-second of the Long Discourses, named, tradition says, for Atanata, the city where the verses were composed. Vessavana recites the protection, and the Buddha consents by silence. In the morning he tells the monks what happened, repeats the verses, and says: learn this protection, master it, remember it. It is for your benefit, for the safety and ease of monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen. What's in the chant? It begins with homage to seven Buddhas, starting with Vipassi, the prince of the four sights from a few weeks back, and ending with Gotama. Then it honors each of the four directions and its guardian king, where the sun rises and where it sets. A protection that begins by naming the awakened, then faces outward, all the way round. The Pali word for these verses is paritta, a protection, a safeguard. And this is one of the roots of a practice you can still hear today. In Theravada countries, monks chant parittas to bless a new house, beside the sick, and in times of danger, sometimes holding a white thread that links everyone present. People understand the protection in different ways: as real help from beings who honor the Buddha, as the power of the truth spoken, or as the calm that comes over a mind that is reminded of what it trusts. The sutta itself simply gives the verses, and asks that they be learned.
screen: `ATANATIYA: THE VERSES FROM ATANATA.` · `HOMAGE TO SEVEN BUDDHAS.` · `FOUR DIRECTIONS, FOUR KINGS.` · `PARITTA: A PROTECTION.` · then, large: `PROTECTION.`

segments.voice: If you chant, you can say, slowly, the homage that opens Theravada chanting: namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa, homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, fully awakened. Three times, the way it's traditionally said. If you'd rather not chant, simply sit and turn your attention, one at a time, to the four directions around you, front, right, behind, left, and feel steady at the center. The bell holds the time.
A protective chant. The Atanatiya verses, given by the Four Great Kings in DN 32, honoring seven Buddhas and the four directions. Today's word.
Your line: protection. Today, when you feel exposed or uneasy, come back to one line you trust, and let it steady you. Day five hundred sixty-five.

options: refuse it: monks need no protection.
consent by silence, then teach it to the monks the next morning.
keep it secret for advanced students.

original.note: Pali paritta: protection, safeguard. the name for protective chants like the Atanatiya verses.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist chanting is just meditation set to a tune.
what it means: some chants are parittas, protections, and DN 32 tells how one was given by the Four Great Kings.
what a scholar hears: the Atanatiya is among the parittas of the Theravada chanting tradition, and its cosmology of four guardian kings is shared across Buddhist Asia.

566.title: Six directions
566.hook: young Sigala bows to the six directions; the Buddha gives the bow a meaning
566.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers teach the Sigalovada Sutta to lay people as a guide to family and social life, and some use the six directions as a way to remember the relationships it describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four kings and a verse for the forest, and your line, protection. What steadied you? Today we start a discourse we'll walk for six days, and it begins with a young man soaking wet. Day five hundred sixty-six.

Early morning, outside Rajagaha. A young householder named Sigala has bathed and, still in wet clothes and with wet hair, he raises his joined hands and bows. To the east. The south. The west. The north. Below. Above. Six directions, one after another. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks him what he's doing. Sigala answers simply: my father, as he was dying, told me to honor the directions. So I do, out of respect for his words. Today: six directions.
screen: `WET HAIR, JOINED HANDS.` → `EAST, SOUTH, WEST, NORTH, BELOW, ABOVE.` → `MY FATHER ASKED ME TO.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't tell Sigala to stop. He doesn't call the custom empty, or his father wrong. He says: that isn't quite how the six directions are honored in the noble discipline. And Sigala, curious, asks: then how? Please teach me. So the Buddha keeps the bow and gives it a meaning. The sutta that follows is the Sigalovada, the advice to Sigala, the thirty-first Long Discourse, which an old commentary calls the householder's discipline. Before the directions, the Buddha clears the ground. A wise person, he says, avoids four ways of acting that stain a life: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying. He avoids four motives for doing wrong, which we'll open tomorrow. And he avoids six ways wealth leaks away, which we'll open the day after. Only then does he return to the bow. The six directions are six relationships. East, the direction of the sunrise, is your parents, who came first. South is your teachers. West is your partner and children. North is your friends. Below are those who work for you. Above are the spiritual teachers in your life. Honor each of them, he says, and each will care for you in return. Notice the move. A grieving son's ritual, done for love of his father, isn't thrown away. It's filled. The same bow, the same six turns. Only now each direction has a face in it.
screen: `HE DOESN'T TELL HIM TO STOP.` · `FIRST, CLEAR THE GROUND.` · `SIX DIRECTIONS, SIX RELATIONSHIPS.` · `THE SAME BOW, WITH FACES IN IT.` · then, large: `SIX DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand or sit facing the morning sun's side, the east. With hands together or simply with a nod, honor your parents, or whoever raised you. Turn to the right, south: your teachers. Behind you, west: your partner, your children, your household. To the left, north: your friends. Then down: people who work with or for you. Then up: anyone who has guided you in what matters most. A face for each. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Six directions. In DN 31 Sigala bows to them for his father's sake, and the Buddha makes them six relationships: parents, teachers, family, friends, workers, guides. Today's word.
Your line: six directions. Today, choose one direction and honor the person in it with one small act: a message, a thank you, a little help. Day five hundred sixty-six.

myth: the Buddha tells Sigala to stop bowing to the directions
he keeps the bow and gives each direction a meaning.
Sigala bowed because his dying father asked him to
he honored the directions out of respect for his father's words.

and 'above' for spiritual teachers.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a young man is bowing to the six directions because his dying father asked him to. what do you say?
options: that the custom is empty and he should stop.
that this isn't quite how the noble discipline honors the directions, and when he asks, teach him.
nothing: walk on into town.
fork.reveal: he keeps Sigala's practice and fills it with meaning: six directions become six relationships.

original.note: Pali disa: direction, quarter. Sigala bows to the six disa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha dismissed old rituals.
what it means: here he keeps the ritual and gives it new content: each direction is a relationship.
what a scholar hears: DN 31 reinterprets a ritual (disa-namassana) in the 'noble discipline' (ariyassa vinaye), a pattern seen elsewhere in the canon with brahmanical practices.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the opening scene and the six directions

567.title: Four motives
567.hook: wrongdoing comes from desire, hate, delusion and fear
567.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present the four agati as a checklist for fairness, and the monastic rules name them as the biases a monk who shares out food or lodging must avoid.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sigala's bow, and your line, six directions. Who did you honor? Today closes a week, and the Buddha asks Sigala to look at why people go wrong. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

A referee calls a foul on the visiting team that wasn't a foul. Why? Maybe he likes the home team. Maybe he can't stand the visiting coach. Maybe he just didn't see it clearly. Or maybe forty thousand people were screaming, and he was afraid. Four possible reasons, and the same bad call. Before the Buddha explains the six directions to Sigala, he names exactly these four. Today: four motives.
screen: `A BAD CALL.` → `LIKING, DISLIKE, CONFUSION, FEAR.` → `THE SAME FOUL.`

segments.voice: In the Sigalovada the Buddha says a wise person does no evil from four motives. From desire. From hate. From delusion. From fear. The Pali calls them agati, wrong courses: four ways the mind goes off the road. Desire bends you toward what you want or who you like. Hate bends you against someone. Delusion means you simply don't see clearly. And fear bends you toward whatever keeps you safe. Notice that last one. Elsewhere the discourses name three roots of harm: greed, hate and delusion. This list adds fear. Plenty of harm isn't done out of malice at all. It's done by someone who was afraid to speak up, or afraid to lose a job, or afraid of a crowd. Then the Buddha puts it in verse. Whoever goes against the Dhamma from desire, hate, fear or delusion, his good name fades, like the moon in the waning half of the month. Whoever doesn't, his good name grows, like the moon in the waxing half. Two pictures, one shrinking, one filling. And the verse is about reputation, a young householder's good name. The same four turn up again in the monastic rules: a monk chosen to share out food or lodging must be one who doesn't follow them. Look back at this week: chosen, not born; what I trust; well proclaimed; the marks of kindness; a protective chant; six directions; and now four reasons a good person might still make a bad call.

segments.voice: Sit, and recall one recent decision you're not proud of. Small is fine: a sharp word, a corner cut, a silence when you should have spoken. Hold it gently. Then ask which motive was at work. Wanting something? Disliking someone? Not seeing clearly? Or fear? Don't judge yourself. Just name it, the way you'd name a bird you spotted. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Four motives. In DN 31: desire, hate, delusion and fear, the four wrong courses that lead good people into bad acts. Today's word.
Your line: four motives. Today, before one important choice, check the four: am I leaning from wanting, dislike, confusion, or fear? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

options: desire.
delusion.

fork.reveal: fear. the Sigalovada names it alongside desire, hate and delusion as a reason good people do wrong.

original.note: Pali agati: wrong course, a way off the road. the four are chanda, dosa, moha and bhaya.

trapdoor: what you thought: wrongdoing comes from bad intentions.
what it means: the Sigalovada names four motives, and one of them is simply fear.
what a scholar hears: the four agati (chanda, dosa, moha, bhaya) recur in the Anguttara (e.g. AN 4.17–20) and the Vinaya names them as the biases an officer of the community must avoid.
